text: Process, by definition, is variance reducing. You're introducing it, because you worry that the variance in your org is too high. You want people to sort of meet a certain standard.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Lenny asks Eeke about finding the right level of process for companies at different stages. Eeke explains her perspective on why process can be problematic - it's designed to reduce variance and create consistency, but this comes at the cost of constraining high performers. She argues that while process brings underperformers up to average, it also brings top performers down to that same average level.
text_ko: 프로세스(process)는 말 그대로 변동(variance)을 줄이는 거예요. 조직 내 변동이 너무 크다고 걱정해서 프로세스를 도입하는 거고요. 사람들한테 대체로 일정한 기준(standard)을 맞추게 하고 싶은 거예요.
text_zh: 流程本身就是为了减少差异性的。你之所以要引入流程，是因为担心组织里各种做法差异太大，希望大家都能达到某个统一的标准。
text_es: Los procesos, por definición, reducen la variabilidad. Los introduces porque te preocupa que haya demasiada inconsistencia en tu organización. Quieres que la gente cumpla con cierto estándar.
key_sentence: Process, by definition, is variance reducing.
original_text: Process, by definition, is variance reducing. You're introducing it, because you worry that the variance in your org is too high. You want people to sort of meet a certain standard. And the cost of that is obviously, while you are reducing the standard and bringing folks up to the average, you're also bringing other folks down to the average.

vocabulary.definition: Variance refers to the degree of difference or deviation from a standard or expected value. It is a statistical measure that indicates how much individual data points in a set differ from the mean.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, variance is often analyzed in financial reports to assess performance against budgets or forecasts, helping organizations identify areas of risk or opportunity.
vocabulary.nuance: While variance can indicate potential issues, it can also highlight areas of innovation or success, depending on the context in which it is analyzed.

vocabulary.definition: A standard is an established norm or requirement that serves as a basis for comparison or judgment. It is often used to ensure quality, consistency, and compliance within processes or products.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, standards are critical for maintaining quality control, ensuring regulatory compliance, and fostering best practices across teams and departments.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'standard' can imply rigidity, but it can also represent a benchmark for excellence, depending on the organization's culture and goals.

vocabulary.definition: Introducing refers to the act of bringing something new into a situation or context, often with the intention of improving or changing existing conditions. It can involve presenting new ideas, products, or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, introducing new initiatives or technologies is essential for innovation and competitiveness, as companies seek to adapt to changing market demands and improve operational efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'introducing' suggests a positive change, it can also imply disruption, especially if stakeholders are resistant to new ideas or processes.

vocabulary.definition: A process is a series of actions or steps taken to achieve a particular end or result. It encompasses the systematic approach to completing tasks or delivering products and services.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, processes are crucial for operational efficiency, as they help streamline workflows, reduce errors, and ensure consistent outcomes across various functions.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'process' can sometimes imply bureaucracy or complexity, but it is also associated with organization and clarity when well-defined.

text: And oftentimes, the folks you're bringing down are your highest performers, your most creative thinkers. The folks who, I think actually don't really need process to do their best work. And so, that, I think is always the tension that you have with process.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Continuing her discussion about organizational process, Eeke explains who gets hurt most by too much process. She identifies that the people most constrained by process are often the highest performers and most creative thinkers - the very people who don't need process to excel. This creates an inherent tension where the tools meant to help the organization can actually hinder its best talent.
text_ko: 그리고 자주 보면, 프로세스(process)를 도입하면서 제약을 받는 사람들은 오히려 성과가 가장 높은 사람들, 가장 창의적인 사람들인 경우가 많아요. 제 생각엔 그분들은 최고의 성과를 내는 데 굳이 프로세스가 필요하지 않은 경우가 많고요. 그래서 그게 프로세스와 늘 생기는 긴장이라고 생각해요.
text_zh: 而且很多时候，你拖累的恰恰是那些表现最好的员工，那些最有创意的人才。我觉得这些人其实根本不需要什么流程就能把工作做得很出色。所以我认为，这就是流程管理永远存在的一个矛盾点。
text_es: Y muchas veces, la gente que terminas frenando son tus mejores elementos, tus pensadores más creativos. La gente que, yo creo, en realidad no necesita procesos para dar lo mejor de sí. Y ahí es donde siempre tienes esa tensión con los procesos.
key_sentence: Bringing down highest performers creates inherent tension with process.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals or teams that consistently achieve exceptional results and exceed expectations in their roles.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, highest performers are often recognized as key contributors to a company's success, driving innovation and productivity.
vocabulary.nuance: This term carries a positive connotation, suggesting not only high output but also the potential for leadership and influence within an organization.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals who generate innovative ideas and solutions, often approaching problems from unique perspectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: Creative thinkers are highly valued in business environments, particularly in roles that require innovation, marketing, and product development.
vocabulary.nuance: While the term is generally positive, it may imply a lack of structure or conventionality, which can be viewed as a drawback in highly regimented environments.

vocabulary.definition: A state of mental or emotional strain resulting from conflicting demands or situations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, tension often arises between the need for structure and process versus the desire for flexibility and creativity among employees.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can suggest a negative atmosphere, but it can also indicate a dynamic environment where differing viewpoints are present and can lead to growth.

vocabulary.definition: A series of actions or steps taken to achieve a particular end or outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: Processes are essential in business for ensuring efficiency, consistency, and quality in operations, often documented in standard operating procedures.
vocabulary.nuance: While processes can enhance productivity, they may also be perceived as restrictive, especially by those who thrive in more fluid, unstructured environments.

text: I say this often actually, to folks who are thinking about going into product management. 'That's awesome. Just be really, really sure about what you're signing up for.' It's kind of the same as, I think a lot of people want to become a manager.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Lenny and Eeke discuss why companies like Stripe were initially hesitant to hire product managers, with engineers preferring to do product work themselves. Eeke warns people considering product management careers about the reality of the role. She compares it to management, where people are attracted to the perceived authority and influence but don't realize much of the actual work involves less glamorous tasks like performance reviews and one-on-ones.
text_ko: 사실 제품 관리(product management)에 뛰어들려고 생각하는 분들에게 저는 이 말을 자주 해요. "정말 멋진 일이에요. 다만, 맡으려는 역할과 책임이 무엇인지 정말정말 확실히 알아두세요." 이건 많은 분들이 매니저가 되고 싶어 하는 경우와도 비슷한 얘기예요.
text_zh: 我其实经常跟那些想转产品经理(product management)的人说，"挺好的，但你得想清楚自己要入的是什么坑。"这就跟很多人想当管理者一样。
text_es: Se los digo mucho a la gente que está pensando en meterse en gestión de productos. "Qué bueno, pero asegúrate muy, muy bien de en qué te estás metiendo." Es como cuando mucha gente quiere volverse manager, ¿no?
key_sentence: Be sure about what you're signing up for in product management.
original_text: I say this often actually, to folks who are thinking about going into product management. 'That's awesome. Just be really, really sure about what you're signing up for.' It's kind of the same as, I think a lot of people want to become a manager. But just so you know, being a manager is like, 'Hey, you're doing performance reviews a lot. And you're in one-on-ones a lot.'

vocabulary.definition: To formally agree to participate in or take on a commitment, often involving a contract or registration process.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'signing up for' can refer to committing to a role, project, or service, indicating a willingness to undertake responsibilities associated with that commitment.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often implies a level of enthusiasm or eagerness, but can also suggest a need for caution if the commitment is significant.

vocabulary.definition: The process of overseeing the development, marketing, and lifecycle of a product, ensuring it meets customer needs and business goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startups, product management is crucial for aligning product features with market demands and coordinating between various teams such as engineering, marketing, and sales.
vocabulary.nuance: This term carries a connotation of leadership and strategic thinking, highlighting the importance of both technical knowledge and customer insight.

text: And I very strongly believe this. I don't think you can be a good writer, unless you're a clear thinker. And if you couldn't write well, I think it was actually pretty hard to be successful at Stripe, at least in the early days.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Lenny asks Eeke what made Stripe's culture unique and successful. Eeke explains Stripe's strong writing culture, where all important communication happened through written documents like business reviews and strategy memos. She argues that good writing and clear thinking are inseparable skills, and Stripe's emphasis on writing quality effectively selected for and developed clear thinkers throughout the organization.
text_ko: 저는 이 점을 정말 강하게 믿어요. 명확하게 생각하지 않으면 좋은 작가가 되기 어렵다고 생각해요. 그리고 글을 잘 쓰지 못하면, 적어도 Stripe 초창기에는 성공하기가 꽤 어려웠을 거예요.
text_zh: 我非常坚信这一点。我觉得思路不清晰的话，是写不出好东西的。在Stripe早期，如果你文笔不行，说实话很难做出成绩来。
text_es: Estoy muy convencido de esto. No creo que puedas ser un buen escritor si no tienes las ideas claras. Y si no sabías escribir bien, la verdad es que era bastante difícil triunfar en Stripe, al menos en los primeros años.
key_sentence: I don't think you can be a good writer, unless you're a clear thinker.
original_text: And I very strongly believe this. I don't think you can be a good writer, unless you're a clear thinker. And if you couldn't write well, I think it was actually pretty hard to be successful at Stripe, at least in the early days. So I think Stripe just cultivated a lot of really good writers, and by input into that, a lot of really good thinkers.

vocabulary.definition: A clear thinker is an individual who can analyze information logically and make sound decisions based on that analysis. This quality is essential for effective problem-solving and strategic planning.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, clear thinkers are valued for their ability to navigate complex challenges and communicate solutions effectively, which is crucial for innovation and leadership.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies not just intelligence but also the ability to articulate thoughts in a straightforward manner, making it a desirable trait in collaborative settings.

vocabulary.definition: Successful refers to achieving desired outcomes or goals, often measured by accomplishments, profitability, or recognition. It indicates a favorable result in a given context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup world, being successful often means securing funding, achieving market traction, or reaching profitability, which are critical for long-term sustainability.
vocabulary.nuance: While success is often associated with financial gain, it can also encompass personal fulfillment and impact, making it a multifaceted concept.

text: I always wonder, 'What is it that's stopping folks from being creative and thinking bigger?' And I think it comes down to a couple of things that companies do sort of unwillingly, or not even realizing it. And one is this fear of failure.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Lenny asks why some teams can innovate consistently while others stay conservative. Rather than focusing on what makes teams innovative, Eeke examines what prevents innovation. She identifies fear of failure as a key barrier, explaining that leaders often want the benefits of innovation but aren't prepared to accept that big swings inevitably lead to some failures. This creates an environment where people avoid taking creative risks.
text_ko: 저는 항상 ‘사람들이 창의적이지 못하고 더 크게 생각하지 못하게 만드는 게 뭘까?’ 하고 궁금해해요. 제 생각에는 그게 회사들이 의도치 않게, 심지어 자신들도 모르게 하는 몇 가지 관행 때문이에요. 그중 하나가 실패에 대한 두려움이에요.
text_zh: 我一直在想，"到底是什么阻碍了大家发挥创造力，让思维变得更开阔？" 我觉得归根结底是公司在做的几件事，而且往往是无意中做的，甚至自己都没意识到。其中一个就是害怕失败。
text_es: Siempre me pregunto: '¿Qué es lo que frena a la gente para ser más creativa y pensar en grande?' Y creo que se debe a un par de cosas que las empresas hacen sin querer, o sin siquiera darse cuenta. Y una de ellas es ese miedo al fracaso.
key_sentence: Fear of failure stops folks from thinking bigger about innovation.
original_text: I always wonder, 'What is it that's stopping folks from being creative and thinking bigger?' And I think it comes down to a couple of things that companies do sort of unwillingly, or not even realizing it. And one is this fear of failure. I think leaders want the upside of innovation, but they're not really willing to deal with the cost of innovation.

vocabulary.definition: A psychological barrier characterized by the apprehension of not achieving desired outcomes, which can hinder decision-making and risk-taking.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and corporate environments, fear of failure can stifle innovation and prevent teams from pursuing bold strategies or experimenting with new ideas.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often implies a deeper emotional response that can affect not only individual performance but also organizational culture.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to the ability to produce original and imaginative ideas or solutions.
vocabulary.businessContext: Creativity is a valuable asset in business, fostering innovation and enabling companies to differentiate themselves in crowded markets.
vocabulary.nuance: While often associated with artistic endeavors, 'creative' in business contexts emphasizes problem-solving and strategic thinking.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of expanding one's perspective to envision larger possibilities and more ambitious goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business strategy, thinking bigger encourages leaders and teams to pursue transformative ideas that can lead to significant growth and impact.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase suggests a proactive mindset and is often used to inspire teams to overcome limitations and embrace expansive thinking.

text: To me, the unlock for organizations is managers, for this.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Lenny asks how to create escape hatches for top performers who are constrained by organizational processes. Eeke explains that managers are the key to solving this problem. Managers must be able to identify high performers who don't need standard processes, then provide 'air cover' - protection from organizational scrutiny - when giving these individuals special treatment and flexibility to work outside normal procedures.
text_ko: 제게는 조직을 바꿀 수 있는 열쇠가 관리자들이에요.
text_zh: 在我看来，要解决这个问题，关键还是得靠管理层。
text_es: Para mí, la clave para las organizaciones en esto son los gerentes.
key_sentence: the unlock for organizations is managers
original_text: To me, the unlock for organizations is managers, for this. Because you need managers to both detect the high performers and be like, 'This person doesn't need the process.' And then you need managers to give that person air cover to be like, 'We're honestly...' Because what you're doing is, you're giving them some special treatment and you need to be kind of okay with that.

vocabulary.definition: To open or make accessible something that was previously restricted or unavailable.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'unlock' often refers to revealing potential or capabilities within an organization, such as unlocking employee performance through effective management.
vocabulary.nuance: The term carries a positive connotation, suggesting the removal of barriers to success or innovation.

vocabulary.definition: Structured groups of people working together to achieve common goals or objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business, organizations can refer to companies, non-profits, or any collective entity that operates within a market or community.
vocabulary.nuance: While often used interchangeably with 'companies,' 'organizations' can also encompass a broader range of entities, including informal groups and associations.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals responsible for overseeing and directing the activities of a team or organization to achieve specific objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, managers play a pivotal role in decision-making, resource allocation, and team leadership, often acting as a bridge between upper management and employees.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can carry varying connotations depending on the management style, ranging from authoritative to collaborative.

text: I have a couple of, I guess, specific mental models that I use. The first is, build for your best user, not your worst user.
speaker: Eeke de Milliano
context: Lenny asks Eeke about product building philosophies she's found useful. Eeke shares her first mental model about user focus. She argues that teams often get distracted by edge cases and potential product abuse, then end up designing awkward features to prevent misuse. Instead, she advocates focusing on the ideal users who will use the product correctly, since poor users should represent only a small fraction of the user base.
text_ko: 저에게는, 음, 몇 가지 특정한 멘탈 모델(mental models)이 있어요. 첫 번째는 최악의 사용자에게 맞춰 만들지 말고 최고의 사용자에게 맞춰 설계하라는 거예요.
text_zh: 我有几个比较具体的思维模式吧。第一个就是，要为你最好的用户去做产品，别老想着那些最难搞的用户。
text_es: Tengo un par de marcos mentales (mental models) que uso bastante. El primero es: diseña para tu mejor usuario, no para el peor.
key_sentence: Build for your best user, not for potential abuse of this product.
original_text: I have a couple of, I guess, specific mental models that I use. The first is, build for your best user, not your worst user. And what I mean by that is, I think it's actually really easy to get stuck, or to focus on, 'What if there's abuse of this product?' Or think about all the ways in which the product won't be used well.

vocabulary.definition: Cognitive frameworks that individuals use to understand and interpret information, guiding their decision-making and problem-solving processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, mental models help leaders and teams to conceptualize complex scenarios, enabling more effective strategy formulation and innovation.
vocabulary.nuance: While mental models can simplify decision-making, they may also lead to biases if not regularly challenged or updated.

vocabulary.definition: To design or create a product or service with a specific target audience or user group in mind.
vocabulary.businessContext: In product development, 'build for' emphasizes the importance of aligning features and functionalities with the needs and preferences of the ideal customer.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase suggests a proactive approach to user experience, contrasting with reactive design that addresses only existing problems.
